Framework five is Regression Discontinuity, or RD. This one works when treatment assignment is based on a score crossing a threshold. In our example, suppose agents with a media engagement score above 70 get targeted for the ad. The key insight is that agents scoring 69 and agents scoring 71 are nearly identical, they just happened to land on different sides of an arbitrary line. So comparing their voting intentions approximates a local randomized experiment. If there is a sharp jump in voting intention right at the cutoff, that is evidence the ad caused it. But, and this is important, the estimate is hyper local. It only tells you the effect for agents near the cutoff of 70. It says nothing about agents scoring 30 or 95. You also have to worry about manipulation. If agents can game their score to get above or below the threshold, the whole design breaks down.

Framework six is Difference in Differences, or DiD. This is a workhorse of policy evaluation. You need data from before and after the treatment, for both a treated group and a control group. In our example, measure voting intention in two synthetic cities before and after the ad airs in City A only. City A shifts up eight points. City B, which never got the ad, shifts up two points on its own, maybe due to a general trend. The DiD estimate is the difference of those differences. Eight minus two equals six percentage points. The critical assumption is parallel trends. Absent the ad, both cities would have followed the same trajectory. If City A also experienced a political scandal during the ad period, that assumption is violated, and your estimate is contaminated. DiD removes time invariant confounders and common time trends, but it cannot handle shocks that hit only one group.
